discovery: Numerical-relativity solution of the binary black hole inspiral, merger and ringdown problem

nominees.name: John G. Baker
nominees.affiliation: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, USA

subfield: Gravitational physics / numerical relativity and gravitational-wave astronomy
motivation: For decades, whether Einstein's equations could be solved numerically for two merging black holes was an open question. In 2005 Pretorius, using generalized harmonic evolution, and independently the groups led by Campanelli and Baker, using the moving-puncture method, produced the first stable simulations of the full inspiral, merger and ringdown. Within months, numerical relativity went from decades of failure to routine computation. It showed what the strongest-field gravitational waves look like and revealed phenomena such as large recoil kicks. These results became the basis of the waveform models used by LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA to detect signals, test general relativity and measure masses and spins across hundreds of mergers. Without them, GW150914 could not have been confidently identified as a binary black hole or compared with theory. This breakthrough turned gravitational-wave detectors into precision observatories of strong-field gravity.
